stories.title: Alliance for Downtown New York Takes 14K SF at 42 Broadway
stories.excerpt: Nonprofit group Alliance For Downtown New York has expanded its Lower Manhattan footprint to 42 Broadway. The Downtown Alliance, which manages the area’s business improvement district, secured a 14,420-square-foot lease at the Financial District tower, according to a recent CBRE office market report. The Downtown Alliance plans to relocate its operations division to the 22-story office building, a spokesperson for the nonprofit told CO. The nonprofit’s corporate headquarters remain housed roughly three blocks north at Silverstein Properties’ 120 Broadway. JLL’s John Wheeler and his team at JLL represented the tenant in the negotiations. A spokesperson for the team did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The lease terms were not disclosed, but office asking rents in Lower Manhattan averaged $61.91 per square foot in July, according to the CBRE report. A spokesperson for the landlord, Avi Schron‘s Cammeby’s International Group, confirmed the recent transaction to CO, adding that the space is still under construction. It was not immediately clear whether Cammeby’s International Group worked with any outside brokers. Cammeby’s 42 Broadway is located near the intersection of Broadway and Morris Street. Appellate service organization Office of the Appellate Defender relocated there in November, joining a tenant roster that includes office suite provider TKO Suites, chiropractor Prestige Health and Wellness, dental practice DDS Group and cafe Gregorys Coffee. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Alliance for Downtown New York leased 14,420 SF at 42 Broadway in Lower Manhattan.
Downtown Alliance relocating operations division; HQ remains at 120 Broadway three blocks north.
Lower Manhattan office asking rents averaged $61.91/SF in July 2024.
stories.summary: The Downtown Alliance, which manages Lower Manhattan's business improvement district, expanded its footprint by leasing 14,420 square feet at 42 Broadway in the Financial District. The nonprofit is moving its operations division to the 22-story tower while maintaining headquarters at 120 Broadway. The transaction reflects sustained office demand in Lower Manhattan, where average asking rents stood at $61.91 per square foot as of July.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. This is an office lease by a nonprofit tenant and signals stable institutional demand in Lower Manhattan, but does not materially affect apartment construction, demand, or financing dynamics in the metro.

stories.title: New York’s Rent Freeze Was Only An Aftershock. This 2019 Law Was The Quake.
stories.excerpt: Jose Tur owns two rent-stabilized rental buildings in Manhattan’s Washington Heights with a total of 45 units. The properties have been in his family for over 30 years, and the mortgages are fully paid off. But Tur tells Commercial Observer that despite this, while he’s reluctant to give an exact number, “more than two or three” units have been sitting empty for an average of over two years. That’s because, according to Tur’s estimates, it would cost anywhere from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit to return them to a livable state, and that’s money he can’t justify spending in return for the stabilized rent amounts in today’s environment. “Some of them require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Tur, who has testified about these financial challenges to New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). “[Oftentimes] the plumbing’s really old because a tenant has lived there for 10 to 15 years, and you have to do the electrical and then lead abatement, which really increases the tally on the job.” Tur says that the $30,000 estimate is before taking into account more cosmetic fixes like cabinets, tiles and so forth, meaning the total is often closer to $60,000 for a one-bedroom apartment. Given all this, the fate of his currently empty apartments is uncertain. With no financial relief in sight, it is likely the units will not be lived in again for the foreseeable future, removed from the rolls of New York’s livable spaces — and from Tur’s income-producing properties — as if they had never existed. The RGB approved a freeze on rent increases for one- and two-year leases for the city’s rent-stabilized apartments in June for lease terms beginning on Oct. 1 or later. bullets: NYC rent-stabilized owner reports 2+ of 45 units vacant 2+ years due to $30K–$60K rehab costs.
2019 rent regulation law (RGB) cap rent growth below rehab economics for small landlords.
Owners unable to justify capital reinvestment under stabilized rent ceilings; units remain offline.
stories.summary: A Manhattan rent-stabilized landlord with 45 units in Washington Heights reports that more than two units have sat vacant for over two years because the cost to restore them to livable standards ($30,000–$60,000 per unit) cannot be recovered under rent-stabilized rents capped by New York's 2019 rent regulation law. Lead abatement, electrical, and plumbing upgrades drive high remediation costs, but RGB-approved rent increases do not justify the capital outlay. The owner's testimony highlights a structural disincentive for supply restoration in the stabilized stock.
stories.impact: Signals accelerating withdrawal of rent-stabilized units from the NYC rental supply pipeline. Stabilized units taken offline reduce overall supply but do not compete with market-rate multifamily development; however, this underscores the regulatory risk and owner-hostile environment in NYC that may deter investor acquisition and development activity in the outer boroughs where stabilized stock concentration is higher.

stories.title: Local Developer Plans to Build a School at 1000 University Avenue in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: School is in session in the Bronx, or at least it will be. Kiumarz Geula, principal of real estate development firm Pillar Property Management, has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to build a seven-story school building at 1000 University Avenue in the Highbridge neighborhood of the Bronx. The plans were filed with the DOB on Aug. 5. Geula did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Jonathan Imani of IMC Architecture, the registered architect on the project, also did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. The DOB plans have few details about the scope of the work coming to the vacant Bronx property. The plans call for the construction of a 64,366-square-foot, 108-foot tall building with a cafeteria and recreation space. No other details are available. Pillar Property Management isn’t the only developer planning to bring a new school building to the Bronx. In June, Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures secured a $60 million debt package to acquire and build a charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue, Commercial Observer reported at the time. Ripco Real Estate’s James Murad, who arranged the financing for that deal, told CO at the time that the project reflects “the growing demand for high-quality educational facilities in underserved communities and the continued appeal of mission-driven real estate investments.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Pillar Property Management filed plans for 64,366 SF, 7-story school at 1000 University Avenue, Highbridge, Bronx.
Apex Development/Knickpoint Ventures also planning charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue with $60M debt.
Bronx school development signals institutional demand for education real estate in underserved neighborhoods.
stories.summary: Pillar Property Management filed plans with NYC Department of Buildings on August 5 to construct a 64,366-square-foot, seven-story school building at 1000 University Avenue in the Highbridge neighborhood of the Bronx. The building will include cafeteria and recreation space. This follows another charter school development by Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures at 1780 East Tremont Avenue, which secured $60 million in debt financing.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. School construction is a separate asset class and does not affect apartment demand or supply. However, the cluster of institutional/educational investment in the Bronx—particularly in Highbridge and Tremont—may signal broader neighborhood investment and population stability that could support future multifamily demand in those submarkets, though this is indirect and long-dated.

stories.title: Gencom Divides Into Two Business Lines With Leadership Promotions
stories.excerpt: Real estate investment firm Gencom is reorganizing into two different business lines, with new hires and promotions to match. The reorganization splits the firm, which has $8 billion in assets under management, into Gencom Capital and Gencom Real Estate, with CEO and founder Karim Alibhai continuing to steer both ships, according to Gencom. Gencom operates up to 6,000 hotel rooms nationwide, including brands like Ritz-Carlton, Rosewood, Auberge Resorts Collection, Fairmont, Hyatt and Marriott. “Successful real estate platforms are built by combining disciplined investing with exceptional execution,” Alibhai said in a statement. “As Gencom continues to grow, this evolution strengthens our leadership, sharpens accountability and positions us to capitalize on the opportunities ahead while continuing to deliver outstanding outcomes for our investors and partners.” Gencom Capital will be led by Chief Investment Officer Alessandro Colantonio, who will handle capital markets, portfolio management and capital allocation. Newly promoted managing directors include Ignasi Puig, who will handle acquisitions and investments; Peter Trujillo, who will be responsible for corporate investments; and Blythe Pierre-Louis, who will manage special situations. Meanwhile, Donald McGregor was promoted to president of Gencom Real Estate and will oversee development, construction and asset management. Shaun Johnston was also promoted to head of portfolio finance and accounting and will report directly to McGregor. Jake Lynch was hired as senior vice president of asset management for Gencom Real Estate. “As we continue to grow, we are building a team with the expertise to create value at every stage of the investment lifecycle,” McGregor said in a statement. “Jake is a terrific addition to the Gencom Real Estate platform, and Shaun’s promotion reflects the depth of talent we have developed within the firm. Together, they reinforce our ability to cultivate ta
bullets: Gencom ($8B AUM) reorganizes into two business lines: Gencom Capital and Gencom Real Estate.
Firm operates 6,000 hotel rooms under luxury brands (Ritz-Carlton, Hyatt, Marriott, Fairmont).
CEO Karim Alibhai retains dual leadership; new COO and CIO hired to sharpen accountability.
stories.summary: Real estate investment firm Gencom, with $8 billion in assets under management, has reorganized into two distinct business lines—Gencom Capital and Gencom Real Estate—with CEO Karim Alibhai leading both. Gencom Capital will focus on capital markets and portfolio management under new Chief Investment Officer Alessandro Colantonio, while Gencom Real Estate will oversee the firm's portfolio of up to 6,000 hotel rooms across luxury brands including Ritz-Carlton, Fairmont, and Hyatt. The restructuring is intended to strengthen leadership and improve accountability.
stories.impact: No direct impact on multifamily development. Gencom is a hospitality-focused firm; the reorganization is an internal capital structure change and does not signal shifts in office conversion pipelines, financing availability, or market demand relevant to apartment development.

stories.title: Real Capital Solutions Launches $350M Distressed Office Acquisition Fund
stories.excerpt: Real Capital Solutions (RCS), a real estate investment firm headquartered in Colorado, has launched a new $350 million fund that will target acquiring distressed Class A and Class B offices across the U.S., Commercial Observer can first report. The fund, RCS Contrarian Office Fund, plans to lever-up and ultimately acquire up to $850 million of office assets from the $350 million raised. The fund is already capitalized through a $50 million personal commitment by Marcel Arsenault, founder and CEO of Real Capital Solutions, and a second $47.5 million commitment from an unnamed entrepreneur. The fund will close in the first quarter of 2027. “While the office market continues to reset, we believe the long-term outlook for premier office assets is extremely strong,” Arsenault said in a statement. “Companies still need high-quality workplaces to attract tenants, foster innovation and drive growth, and those assets will continue to outperform over time.” This is not the first time RCS has jumped into pools of office distress. Since 2024, the firm has invested $644 million into acquiring 14 office properties in 10 U.S. markets — buildings that include Walnut Glen Tower and Tower at Park Lane in Dallas; Belleview Tower in Denver; Tysons Pointe in Northern Virginia; 101 Marietta Street in Atlanta; and the Equitable Building in Chicago, a 35-story Class A office tower the firm acquired earlier this year for $132.5 million, or a 77.8 percent discount to replacement cost. bullets: Real Capital Solutions launched $350M distressed office fund; plans to lever 2.4x to $850M acquisition capacity.
RCS Contrarian Office Fund targets Class A and Class B office distress nationwide.
CEO Marcel Arsenault committed $50M personal capital; second investor committed $47.5M.
stories.summary: Real Capital Solutions (RCS), headquartered in Colorado, launched a new $350 million fund—the RCS Contrarian Office Fund—targeting distressed Class A and Class B office assets across the U.S. The fund plans to use leverage to acquire up to $850 million in office assets. Founder and CEO Marcel Arsenault committed $50 million personally, and an unnamed entrepreneur committed $47.5 million. RCS is betting that premium office assets will outperform long-term despite current market headwinds.
stories.impact: Moderate capital signal, not a direct demand driver for multifamily. The fund's formation reflects conviction that office distress creates acquisition opportunities, but it does NOT redirect capital to multifamily development. However, it does indicate that institutional capital remains deployed in real estate despite uncertainty, and may compete for debt financing and investor equity that could otherwise flow to apartment development. Monitor whether this fund's success in office distress leads to similar strategies in residential or signals capital reallocation away from multifamily in 2025.
